# Bounds for inertialess dynamo

**Authors:** Ali Arslan Address: AA: Institute of Geophysics ETH Zürich Zürich, CH-8092, Switzerland Email address: ali.arslan@eaps.ethz.ch and Hezekiah Grayer II Address: HG: Program in Applied & Computational Mathematics Princeton University Princeton, NJ 08544, USA Email address: hgrayer@math.princeton.edu In memory of Dr. John Bryan Taylor

## Abstract

We derive necessary conditions for instantaneous dynamo action for rotating convection. A magnetohydrodynamic model is considered in two settings: the rapidly rotating plane layer where inertia and viscosity are absent, and at an arbitrary rotation rate where viscosity is finite. In contrast to kinematic dynamo bounds, the evolution of the magnetic field is coupled via an inertialess force balance. The buoyancy-driven part of the flow $\bm{u}^{\mathrm{A}}$ in the event of dynamo action must in fact satisfy, for $3\leq p\leq\infty$

where $A_{p}$ is an explicit constant, and $Rm$ is the magnetic Reynolds number. In the inviscid model, $\bm{u}^{\mathrm{A}}$ depends only on the horizontal gradients of the vertical primitive of temperature. A refinement via the poloidal-toroidal decomposition allows us to replace $L^{p}$ in our constraint with an anisotropic norm for $L^{\infty}_{z}\dot{H}^{1}_{x,y}$ . For the viscous model, we also derive necessary conditions for the growth of magnetic enstrophy and a combined thermo-magnetic energy. One branch of our constraints implies that the scaling $\mbox{{Ra}}_{\nu}\gtrsim Ek^{-3/2}$ is necessary for dynamo action, where $\mbox{{Ra}}_{\nu}$ is the classical Rayleigh number and $Ek$ is the Ekman number.

## 1. Introduction

The Earth, several other planets, and the Sun all possess large scale magnetic fields driven by the motion of an electrically conducting fluid under convection. The Earth’s magnetic field is aperiodic, undergoing secular variation and reversals, and the other planetary magnetic fields across the Solar System exhibit considerable temporal and morphological diversity; see [RK13, KR02, Mof08, Dav+15] and [Jon11, SS11, TE22, Sod+25].

Understanding which balance of forces and parameter regimes are necessary for dynamo action remains a central problem in dynamo theory [Yad+16, SGA19]. A basic model for the force balance is the magnetohydrodynamic equations under the Boussinesq approximation [BR95, Dor24]. Planetary magnetic fields are expected to be generated by a rapidly rotating dynamo, where inertial and viscous forces are relatively small [SGA19]. This force hierarchy can be investigated by direct numerical simulations, but the parameters relevant to planets are beyond the current capabilities of computational methods [Lan+22]. In this paper, we address mathematically the basic question: what conditions are necessary for dynamo action in an inertialess dynamo?

### 1.1. Contribution

We first consider the Taylor limit, in which inertia and viscosity are absent from the force balance, in a horizontally periodic plane layer with either boundary or internal heating; see [Tay63] and [HC16, CH06, HC19, CH17, Jon91]. We show that critical to dynamo action is the contribution of the buoyancy-driven part of the flow, i.e., the Archimedean part of the fluid velocity

$$ \bm{u}^{\mathrm{A}}(x,y,z)=\mbox{{Ra}}\,\nabla_{x,y}^{\perp}\int_{0}^{z}T(x,y,z^{\prime})\,\mathrm{d}z^{\prime} $$

where Ra is the modified Rayleigh number. More precisely, we prove that for $3\leq p\leq\infty$ instantaneous growth of the magnetic energy requires

$$ \mbox{{Rm}}\,A_{p}\|\bm{u}^{A}\|_{L^{p}}=\mbox{{Rm}}\,\mbox{{Ra}}\,A_{p}\|\nabla_{x,y}\overline{T}\|_{L^{p}}\geq 1 $$

where $\overline{T}$ is the vertical primitive of the temperature, $A_{p}$ is a constant, and Rm is the magnetic Reynolds number. We refine the above bound via the poloidal-toroidal decomposition of the magnetic field to replace $L^{p}$ with the anisotropic $L_{z}^{\infty}\dot{H}^{1}_{x,y}$ . Further, we prove absorbing ball estimates for the temperature equation wherein we determine explicit regions of parameter space in which magnetic energy growth is prohibited in long-time convection.

We then extend the analysis to the viscous inertialess problem with finite the Ekman number $Ek>0$ and stress-free velocity boundary conditions. The condition for dynamo action is robust and holds with finite viscosity corrections, showing that the restriction on the Archimedean response is not reliant on singular properties of Taylor’s constraint. The constraint naturally yields the scaling $Ra_{\nu}\gtrsim Ek^{-3/2}$ , where $Ra_{\nu}$ is the classical Rayleigh number in the study of convection. In addition to magnetic energy, we prove a constraint for the growth of magnetic enstrophy and a combined thermo-magnetic energy. The growth condition for the combined energy in a rapidly rotating solution branch again has the scaling $Ra_{\nu}\gtrsim Ek^{-3/2}$ .

### 1.2. Magneto-geostrophic models

The inviscid model considered in this paper was studied by J. B. Taylor in his seminal work on the geodynamo [Tay63]. Taylor observed that when inertia and viscosity are absent, for a fluid in a self gravitating sphere, the total magnetic torque on every geostrophic cylinder centred on the rotation axis must vanish. This condition is now known as Taylor’s constraint [Jon91]. Equivalently, the Lorentz force must lie in the range of the Coriolis operator after projection onto solenoidal vector fields [GG17]. The constraint is one of the main reasons why the Taylor dynamo is mathematically delicate. At each instant, the magnetostrophic and buoyancy driven components of the velocity are constrained, whereas the geostrophic component is not determined by the instantaneous force balance alone [WBJ98, Mof08, LJL18]. Taylor proposed that the requirement of remaining on the constraint manifold determines this geostrophic flow, but the original prescription was later shown to be insufficient in general three-dimensional Taylor states due to an incorrect evaluation of the boundary data in spherical domains [Har+18].

At finite viscosity, $Ek>0$ , viscous forces regularise the degeneracy of the Taylor limit. This viscous inertialess problem has formed the basis of several plane layer studies, including computations observing weak- and strong-field dynamo states [JR00, CH17, HC19, HC16]. Realistic $Ek\ll 1$ remain computationally inaccessible by direct numerical simulations. Instead, a ‘Taylorisation coefficient’ has been used to measure the degree to which Taylor’s constraint is satisfied as $Ek$ decreases [SH04, RJ02]. We consider both the singular Taylor limit and its finite viscosity extension.

The solution theory of the Taylor model is incomplete. Well-posedness is subtle even for perturbative variants [ML94, FV11a, FV11, FRV12, FS15, GG17]. However, the instantaneous force balance still imposes useful constraints. In particular, identities associated with the Coriolis operator allow magnetic energy production to be related to the horizontal Archimedean flow generated by buoyancy, without determining the subsequent evolution of the geostrophic flow. We can therefore ask: for smooth solutions of Taylor’s model, what quantitative conditions are necessary for magnetic energy or magnetic enstrophy to grow?

### 1.3. Kinematic dynamo theory

Previous rigorous studies of dynamo action are restricted to kinematic dynamos. Kinematic dynamos are simplifications in which magnetic feedback on the flow is neglected [Mof78]. In this setting, the velocity field, $\bm{u}$ , is determined independently of the magnetic field. The induction equation then becomes a linear evolution equation for the magnetic field, and dynamo action is formulated as the existence of magnetic fields with a positive asymptotic growth rate under the action of the induction operator. The study of kinematic dynamos is diverse [DJ89, Gub08, Ale11, Gal12, Rin19, Kla92, FV91], here we review the results relevant to our subsequent nonlinear study.

The first major antidynamo result is due to Cowling [Cow33] and states that an axisymmetric magnetic field vanishing at infinity cannot be maintained by dynamo action. A Cartesian analogue of Cowling’s theorem states that a magnetic field invariant in one Cartesian direction and decaying appropriately at infinity cannot be maintained. This restriction on magnetic field geometry is distinct from Zel’dovich’s theorem, which prohibits dynamo action driven by a planar two dimensional velocity field in an unbounded domain [Zel57]. A related result is that a purely toroidal flow cannot generate a dynamo; however, if a small poloidal flow exists, a kinematic dynamo requires a sufficiently large toroidal flow [Pro04]. Nuances to the axisymmetric theorems have also been shown to exist [KT14, Kai18, AM21].

Antidynamo theorems exclude exact geometries. A complementary approach excludes flows that are too weak, by deriving necessary lower bounds on $Rm$ . The first result due to Childress [Chi69] applies to velocity fields normalised by their maximum, in which case, $Rm\geq\pi$ , whereas if the maximum strain, $\nabla\bm{u}$ , of the flow is chosen as the velocity scale, $Rm\geq\pi^{2}$ [Bac58]. Both results can be improved for insulating boundary conditions requiring continuity of the wall normal magnetic field to a potential field in the exterior, thereby increasing the minimal necessary $Rm$ to $3.51$ and $12.29$ [Pro77]. In spherical domains, with a radially weighted maximum norm, Kaiser & Tilgner demonstrate that for a selection of velocity fields, the lower bounds are improved by a factor of up to 2.6 [KT25].

By contrast, if the velocity is normalised by an $L^{2}$ norm, there is no positive universal lower bound on $Rm$ . A result demonstrated by constructing a class of flows with decreasing minimum $Rm$ under a fixed energy norm [Pro15]. However, when the velocity is normalised in an $L^{p}$ norm with $3\leq p\leq\infty$ , then Luo et al. [Luo+20] proved that $Rm\geq\pi^{\frac{6-n}{2n}}(3^{-1/2}(2\pi^{-1})^{2/3})^{\frac{6-3n}{2n}}$ where $2\leq n\leq 6$ and $1/n+1/p=1/2$ . Their result for $n=2$ and $p=\infty$ is equivalent to the original result of Childress, while for $n=6$ and $p=3$ it gives $2.34$ . The authors also find that, under an $L^{2}$ enstrophy normalisation, $Rm\geq 3.1$ [Luo+20].

Kinematic dynamo theory has limited application to the magneto-geostrophic models discussed in §1.2 because the geostrophic component of the flow is typically difficult to compute. Crucially, our constraints for dynamo action do not require information from geostrophic component.

### 1.4. Outline

The paper is organised as follows. In §2 we introduce the dynamo model and Taylor’s constraint. §3 states the main results, first for the Taylor limit and then for the viscous inertialess model. In §4 we present bounds for the temperature equation and use them to simplify the results of the previous section in terms of "classical" Rayleigh numbers. §5, 6 and 7 contain the proofs of the inviscid, viscous and temperature equation results. §8 provides concluding remarks. The appendices collect constants and identities of the poloidal-toroidal decomposition.

## 2. Governing Equations

We consider an electrically conducting fluid confined by two horizontal parallel plates in a rotating frame of reference. The frame rotates at a rate $\Omega$ and gravity acts antiparallel to the vertical direction with strength $g$ .

The fluid is considered incompressible and has density $\rho$ . The fluid has kinematic viscosity $\nu$ . For thermal properties, the fluid has thermal diffusivity $\kappa$ , specific heat capacity $c_{p}$ and thermal expansion coefficient $\alpha$ . As a conductor, the fluid has electrical conductivity $\sigma$ and permeability $\mu$ . The plates are separated by a distance $d$ , and are periodic in the horizontal directions with periods $L_{x}d$ and $L_{y}d$ . The fluid is subject to internal or boundary heating.

### 2.1. Inertialess Magnetohydrodynamics

*Figure 1. Schematic diagram of our dynamo configuration. The fluid is bounded between two horizontal plates and the domain is periodic in the $x$ and $y$ directions. The frame rotates about the $z$ axis at a constant rate $\Omega$ and $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity. The magnetic field $\bm{B}$ generated by the fluid is illustrated with blue lines.*

To nondimensionalise the problem, we fix $d$ as the characteristic length scale, $U$ as the velocity scale, $B_{0}$ as the magnetic field scale, and $T_{0}$ as the temperature scale. In nondimensional terms, the electrically conducting fluid fills a domain $V=[0,L_{x}]\times[0,L_{y}]\times[0,1]$ and is described by the magnetohydrodynamic equations

$$ \displaystyle\bm{e}_{z}\times\bm{u}+\nabla P-\mbox{{Ek}}\nabla^{2}\bm{u} \displaystyle=\Lambda(\nabla\times\bm{B})\times\bm{B}+\mbox{{Ra}}\,T\bm{e}_{z}, \displaystyle\nabla\cdot\bm{u} \displaystyle=0, \displaystyle\partial_{t}\bm{B}-\nabla\times(\bm{u}\times\bm{B}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\mbox{{Rm}}}\nabla^{2}\bm{B}, \displaystyle\nabla\cdot\bm{B} \displaystyle=0, \displaystyle\partial_{t}T+\nabla\cdot(\bm{u}T) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\mbox{{Pe}}}\nabla^{2}T+\frac{Q}{\mbox{{Pe}}}. $$

The equations are inertialess having taken the limit $\mbox{{Ro}}\to 0$ , where $Ro$ is the Rossby number. The nondimensional parameters, and their role in the model, are detailed below.

The unknowns are the fluid velocity, the magnetic field, and the temperature:

$$ \bm{u}=\sum_{i\in\{x,y,z\}}u_{i}(\bm{x},t)\bm{e}_{i},\quad\bm{B}=\sum_{i\in\{x,y,z\}}B_{i}(\bm{x},t)\bm{e}_{i},\quad T=T(\bm{x},t). $$

The internal heating

$$ Q=Q(\bm{x}), $$

is nondimensionalized by $T_{0}$ .

Imposed on these functions are periodicity in $x$ and $y$ , and boundary conditions on $\partial V=\{z=0\}\cup\{z=1\}$ . On the boundaries $S_{\pm}=\{z=1/2\pm 1/2\}$ the outward unit normal is $\bm{n}_{\pm}=\pm\bm{e}_{z}$ . The boundaries are impenetrable, ferromagnetic and isothermal. In the inviscid limit $\mbox{{Ek}}\to 0$ , the boundary conditions are

$$ \displaystyle\bm{u}\cdot\bm{n}_{\pm}\,|_{\,S_{\pm}} \displaystyle=0, \displaystyle\bm{B}\times\bm{n}_{\pm}\,|_{\,S_{\pm}} \displaystyle=0, \displaystyle T\,|_{\,S_{\pm}} \displaystyle=T_{\pm}. $$

In the viscous case $\mbox{{Ek}}>0$ , the fluid satisfies the stress-free condition

$$ (\nabla\times\bm{u})\times\bm{n}_{\pm}\,|_{\,S_{\pm}}=0. $$

The ferromagnetic boundary condition for the magnetic field (2.4b) implies

$$ \displaystyle(\nabla\times\bm{B})\cdot\bm{n}_{\pm}\,|_{\,S_{\pm}} \displaystyle=0, \displaystyle\partial_{z}\bm{B}\cdot\bm{n}_{\pm}\,|_{\,S_{\pm}} \displaystyle=0. $$

The boundary values $T_{+}$ and $T_{-}$ are constant temperatures.

The model is completed with initial conditions for $\bm{B}$ and $T$ . As our analysis is independent of this data, given it is compatible, we do not detail this point.

#### 2.1.1. Nondimensional parameters

From the dimensional parameters defined in the previous section the magnetic diffusivity can be defined as $\eta=1/(\sigma\mu)$ .

The nondimensional numbers are

$$ \begin{array}[]{r l}\text{Rossby:}&\mbox{{Ro}}=U/(2\Omega d)\\
\text{Ekman:}&\mbox{{Ek}}=\nu/(2\Omega d^{2})\\
\text{Elsasser:}&\Lambda=B_{0}^{2}/(2\Omega\rho\mu Ud)\\
\text{(modified) Rayleigh:}&\mbox{{Ra}}=T_{0}\alpha g/(2\Omega U)\\
\text{magnetic Reynolds:}&\mbox{{Rm}}=Ud/\eta\\
\text{Peclet:}&\mbox{{Pe}}=Ud/\kappa.\end{array} $$

For arbitrary $U$ , one observes that the six parameters are independent. The rapid rotation limit $\mbox{{Ro}}\to 0$ is taken to obtain (2.1). Five parameters remain free.

By specifying Rm or Pe, the timescale may be fixed to obtain various rotating magnetohydrodynamic and convective settings considered in the literature:

- (1) magnetic diffusive timescale (2.8)

$$ \mbox{{Rm}}=1\quad\Rightarrow\quad\begin{cases}\Lambda=B_{0}^{2}/(2\Omega\rho\mu\eta)\\ \mbox{{Ra}}=T_{0}\alpha gd/(2\Omega\eta)\\ \mbox{{Pe}}=\eta/\kappa\end{cases}, $$

- (2) thermal diffusive timescale (2.9)

$$ \,\,\mbox{{Pe}}=1\quad\Rightarrow\quad\begin{cases}\Lambda=B_{0}^{2}/(2\Omega\rho\mu\kappa)\\ \mbox{{Ra}}=T_{0}\alpha gd/(2\Omega\kappa)\\ \mbox{{Rm}}=\kappa/\eta\end{cases}. $$

The ratio between these two time scales is the Roberts number defined as

$$ \begin{array}[]{r l}\text{Roberts:}&q=\kappa/\eta.\end{array} $$

#### 2.1.2. Convection settings

We consider two scenarios to drive the temperature field in our governing equations.

- (1) Rayleigh–Bénard convection (2.11)

$$ T_{0}=\tilde{T}_{+}-\tilde{T}_{-},\quad T_{+}=0,\quad T_{-}=1. $$

- (2) Internally heated convection (2.12)

$$ T_{0}=\frac{\tilde{Q}d^{2}}{\rho c_{p}\kappa},\quad T_{+}=0,\quad T_{-}=0. $$

$\tilde{T}_{+}-\tilde{T}_{-}$ is the dimensional temperature difference between the two boundaries, and $\tilde{Q}$ is the dimensional volumetric heating rate such that $Q$ is equal to $\tilde{Q}$ normalised by its norm. In Rayleigh–Bénard, one may consider perturbations of temperature about the conductive state so that the boundary conditions are homogeneous.

### 2.2. Taylor’s Constraint

#### 2.2.1. Mechanical setting

The main result of [Tay63] was the demonstration of a constraint on the flow for regular solutions to the inviscid equations, $\mbox{{Ek}}\to 0$ . Denote the Lorentz force

$$ \bm{F}^{\mathrm{M}}=(\nabla\times\bm{B})\times\bm{B}. $$

Taylor’s constraint is a direct consequence of the balance of torques obtained from the curl of the momentum balance (2.1a) at $\mbox{{Ek}}=0$ ,

$$ -\nabla\times\bm{F}^{\mathrm{M}}=\frac{1}{\Lambda}\left(\mbox{{Ra}}\,\nabla T\times\bm{e}_{z}+\partial_{z}\bm{u}\right). $$

In particular, there is zero torsion on geostrophic surfaces. For the spherical domain originally considered in [Tay63], the geostrophic surfaces are cylinders centered on the axis of rotation.

For the plane layer, the geostrophic surfaces are the vertical extension of any simple closed plane curve $C$ . More precisely, for any simple closed contractible plane curve $C$ in $[0,L_{x}]\times[0,L_{y}]$ any regular solution to equations (2.1) at $\mbox{{Ek}}=0$ must satisfy

$$ \int_{0}^{1}\mathrm{d}z\oint_{C}\bm{F}^{\mathrm{M}}\cdot\mathrm{d}l=0. $$

where in our notation $\mathrm{d}l=(X^{\prime},Y^{\prime},0)\,\mathrm{d}s$ for a parameterization $s\mapsto(X(s),Y(s))$ of the curve $C$ by arc length $s$ . To see this, first integrate the $z$ component of the torque equation (2.14) with respect to $\mathrm{d}z$ and recall that $u_{z}$ vanishes at the boundaries to find

$$ \int_{0}^{1}\bm{e}_{z}\cdot\nabla\times\bm{F}^{\mathrm{M}}\,\mathrm{d}z=0. $$

Integrating (2.16) with respect to $\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y$ the planar region $A\subset[0,L_{x}]\times[0,L_{y}]$ bounded by $C$ such that $\partial A=C$ , the planar Kelvin–Stokes theorem then implies (2.15). In this regard, the torque balance in equation (2.14) is the differential version of Taylor’s constraint. Our main results are derived from this torque balance.

#### 2.2.2. Functional setting

The basic framework for the study of the dynamo problem is the space of finite energy solenoidal fields. For two vector fields $\bm{v}$ and $\bm{w}$ (not necessarily solenoidal), we denote the inner product

$$ \langle\bm{v},\bm{w}\rangle=\int\bm{v}\cdot\bm{w}\,\mathrm{d}V. $$

The space $L^{2}_{\mathrm{sol}}=L^{2}_{\mathrm{sol}}(\mathrm{d}V)$ consists of finite energy solenoidal vector fields, i.e. vector fields $\bm{v}$ such that $\nabla\cdot\bm{v}=0$ and which are finite in the norm

$$ \|\bm{v}\|_{2}=\sqrt{\langle\bm{v},\bm{v}\rangle}. $$

With the inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ , the function space $L^{2}_{\mathrm{sol}}$ is a natural Hilbert space.

Taylor’s constraint has an abstract interpretation via Hilbert space structure. First outlined by Gallagher–Gérard-Varet [GG17], we review briefly the function analytic implications. Denote the Coriolis operator on $L^{2}_{\mathrm{sol}}$

$$ {C}u=\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{sol}}(\bm{e}_{z}\times\bm{u}) $$

where $\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{sol}}$ is the Leray projector onto solenoidal vector fields. Taylor’s constraint (2.15) is equivalent to the condition

$$ \mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{sol}}\bm{F}^{\mathrm{M}}\in\mathrm{Range}\,{C}. $$

The operator ${C}$ is skew-symmetric and linear. A solution $\bm{u}\in L^{2}_{\mathrm{sol}}$ therefore admits a decomposition into magnetostrophic, Archimedean, and geostrophic parts. Each part as follows is in $L^{2}_{\mathrm{sol}}$ , i.e. is solenoidal and tangent to $\partial V$ .

- • The magnetostrophic part $\bm{u}^{\mathrm{M}}$ solves (2.21)

$$ \frac{1}{\Lambda}(\bm{e}_{z}\times\bm{u}^{\mathrm{M}}+\nabla P^{\mathrm{M}})=(\nabla\times\bm{B})\times\bm{B}=\bm{F}^{\mathrm{M}}. $$

- • The Archimedean part $\bm{u}^{\mathrm{A}}$ solves (2.22)

$$ \frac{1}{\mbox{{Ra}}}(\bm{e}_{z}\times\bm{u}^{\mathrm{A}}+\nabla P^{\mathrm{A}})=T\bm{e}_{z}=\bm{F}^{\mathrm{A}}. $$

- • The geostrophic part $\bm{u}^{\mathrm{g}}$ solves (2.23)

$$ \bm{e}_{z}\times\bm{u}^{\mathrm{g}}+\nabla P^{\mathrm{g}}=0. $$

The solenoidal constraint on each part is enforced by their respective pressures.

By the linearity of ${C}$ , it is clear that $\bm{u}=\bm{u}^{\mathrm{M}}+\bm{u}^{\mathrm{A}}+\bm{u}^{\mathrm{g}}$ satisfies the equation (2.1a) in the inviscid limit $\mbox{{Ek}}\to 0$ . At any given instant of time, Taylor’s constraint guarantees the uniqueness of

$$ \bm{u}^{\mathrm{M}},\bm{u}^{\mathrm{A}}\in\{\bm{v}\in L^{2}_{\mathrm{sol}}:\bm{v}(x,y,0)=0\}=\mathcal{G} $$

given their forces are sufficiently regular. The geostrophic part

$$ \bm{u}^{\mathrm{g}}\in\mathrm{Ker}\,{C} $$

is not determined by the requirement (2.20) at a particular time. While the space of particular solutions $\mathcal{G}$ is not exactly the orthogonal complement of $\mathrm{Ker}\,{C}$ , it is the case $\mathcal{G}\cap\mathrm{Ker}\,{C}=0$ and our decomposition is well-defined. Taylor argues that demanding the evolution remains on the (Hilbert) manifold defined by (2.20) is sufficient to determine $\bm{u}^{\mathrm{g}}$ . The argument was revisited in [Har+18] and was found to be incomplete.

By the skew-symmetry of ${C}$ , it follows that the Lorentz and Archimedean forces cannot do work on the flows they generate, nor on geostrophic flows. One verifies that

$$ \langle\bm{u}^{\mathrm{M}},\bm{F}^{\mathrm{M}}\rangle=0,\qquad\langle\bm{u}^{\mathrm{A}},\bm{F}^{\mathrm{A}}\rangle=0, $$

and

$$ \langle\bm{u}^{\mathrm{g}},\bm{F}^{\mathrm{M}}\rangle=0,\qquad\langle\bm{u}^{\mathrm{g}},\bm{F}^{\mathrm{A}}\rangle=0. $$

In the sequel, we shall use pointwise no-work requirements derived from equations (2.21), (2.22) and (2.23). We refer to this procedure as the MAC decomposition.

## 3. Inertialess Dynamo Theorems

The governing equations (2.1) are considered both with and without the effects of viscosity. In particular, we discover requirements for instantaneous magnetic energy non-decay. For nontrivial magnetic field $\bm{B}$ , we specify two notions:

#### Definition 3.1.

Dynamo action occurs if

$$ \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(\frac{1}{2}\int|\bm{B}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}V\right)\geq 0. $$

#### Definition 3.2.

Magnetic flux is exact if

$$ \int\bm{n}_{\pm}\cdot\bm{B}\,\mathrm{d}S_{\pm}=0. $$

The exact condition that the magnetic flux through the boundaries is net-zero is specified to simplify the bounds. It holds automatically in spherical domains.

The section contains three main results: the first is a lower bound on Ra and Rm that does not differentiate the structure of the magnetic field, the second is a bound that does, and the third is a result where $Ek>0$ .

The bounds we discover depend on the quantity

$$ \overline{T}(x,y,z)=\int_{0}^{z}T(x,y,z^{\prime})\,\mathrm{d}z^{\prime}. $$

### 3.1. Taylor Dynamo Theory

In the first subsection, we present our requirements for dynamo action in the inviscid limit $Ek\to 0$ , i.e. the Taylor model for the Earth’s dynamo. In the plane layer, the Taylor model is

$$ \displaystyle\bm{e}_{z}\times\bm{u}+\nabla P \displaystyle=\Lambda(\nabla\times\bm{B})\times\bm{B}+\mbox{{Ra}}\,T\bm{e}_{z}, \displaystyle\nabla\cdot\bm{u} \displaystyle=0, \displaystyle\partial_{t}\bm{B}-\nabla\times(\bm{u}\times\bm{B}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\mbox{{Rm}}}\nabla^{2}\bm{B}, \displaystyle\nabla\cdot\bm{B} \displaystyle=0, $$

and the boundary conditions are

$$ \displaystyle\bm{u}\cdot\bm{n}\,|_{\,S_{\pm}} \displaystyle=0, \displaystyle\bm{B}\times\bm{n}\,|_{\,S_{\pm}} \displaystyle=0, $$

The requirements for dynamo described in this subsection are independent of the temperature model, and so we omit its description here. Taylor’s constraint and the functional setting in Section 2.2 hold in the inviscid model.

The inviscid model (3.2) admits the basic energy identity

$$ \frac{1}{2}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\int|\bm{B}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}V+\frac{1}{\mbox{{Rm}}}\int|\nabla\times\bm{B}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}V=\frac{\mbox{{Ra}}}{\Lambda}\int\bm{u}\cdot T\bm{e}_{z}\,\mathrm{d}V. $$

The production of magnetic energy is strictly determined by the term on the right hand side. Dynamo action is impossible in the pure magnetostrophic limit $\mbox{{Ra}}\to 0$ . Therefore, buoyancy must be significant relative to the Coriolis force for dynamo action to occur, and this ratio is measured by the modified Rayleigh number $\mbox{{Ra}}>0$ .

Our main results are quantitative lower bound on Ra.

#### 3.1.1. Childress-type Bounds

Our bounds are in terms of $L^{p}$ norms and a constant $A_{p}$ . The constant $A_{p}$ depends on the power $p$ and interpolates between $C_{\mathrm{S}}=A_{3}$ from the Sobolev embedding and $C_{\mathrm{P}}=A_{\infty}$ from the Poincaré inequality.

#### Theorem 3.1.

Consider the Taylor model, and suppose that the magnetic flux is exact. Then, for dynamo action it is necessary that, for $3\leq p\leq\infty$ ,

$$ \mbox{{Ra}}\,A_{p}\|\nabla_{x,y}\overline{T}\|_{L^{p}}\geq\frac{1}{\mbox{{Rm}}}. $$

See Section 5.1 for the proof. This bound and the ones to follow are in terms of the horizontal gradient $\nabla_{x,y}$ of the field $\overline{T}$ . In fact, $\overline{T}$ is related to the streamfunction of the Archimedean part of velocity $\bm{u}^{\mathrm{A}}$ (see Section 2.2). Indeed, $\bm{u}^{\mathrm{A}}$ is an entirely horizontal flow and has the explicit form

$$ \bm{u}^{\mathrm{A}}=\mbox{{Ra}}\,\bm{e}_{z}\times\nabla\overline{T}=\mbox{{Ra}}\,\nabla_{x,y}^{\perp}\overline{T}. $$

#### Theorem 3.2.

Consider the Taylor model, and suppose that the magnetic flux is exact. Then, for dynamo action it is necessary that, for $3\leq p\leq\infty$ ,

$$ A_{p}\|\bm{u}^{\mathrm{A}}\|_{L^{p}}\geq\frac{1}{\mbox{{Rm}}}. $$

In the basic energy identity, it is immediate that production of the magnetic energy depends only on the vertical (poloidal) component of the velocity; however, our Theorems claim the significance of an entirely horizontal (toroidal) part of the flow. Rather than conflict, the two observations are in fact commensurate via Taylor’s constraint (see Section 2.2). The production of magnetic energy is exactly

$$ \frac{\mbox{{Ra}}}{\Lambda}\langle\bm{u},\bm{F}^{\mathrm{A}}\rangle=\frac{\mbox{{Ra}}}{\Lambda}\langle\bm{u}^{\mathrm{M}},\bm{F}^{\mathrm{A}}\rangle=\frac{1}{\Lambda}\langle\bm{u}^{\mathrm{M}},\bm{e}_{z}\times\bm{u}^{\mathrm{A}}\rangle=-\langle\bm{u}^{\mathrm{A}},\bm{F}^{\mathrm{M}}\rangle. $$

The identity starts with the right hand side of (3.4), then uses the skew-symmetry of the Coriolis operator and properties of the MAC decomposition; see Section 5.1 for the proof. This identity also clarifies why our bounds are independent of $\Lambda$ .

#### Remark 3.1.

Theorem 3.1 and Theorem 3.2 are equivalent in statement, but not in proof. There is an explicit correction to Theorem 3.1 when viscosity is finite. On the other hand, Theorem 3.2 holds verbatim in a spherical domain for the analogous Archimedean velocity.

#### 3.1.2. Poloidal-Toroidal Decomposition

In this section, we decompose the magnetic field into its poloidal and toroidal components and refine our Childress-type bounds. Our refined bounds are in terms of the anisotropic norm

$$ \|\bm{v}\|_{L^{\infty}_{z}L^{2}_{x,y}}=\sup_{z}\left(\int|\bm{v}(x,y,z)|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y\right)^{1/2}. $$

We state the result first and then discuss the poloidal-toroidal decomposition.

#### Theorem 3.3.

Consider the Taylor model, and suppose that the magnetic flux is exact. For dynamo action, it is necessary that

$$ \mbox{{Ra}}\,A_{2}\,\|\nabla^{2}_{x,y}\overline{T}\|_{L^{\infty}_{z}L^{2}_{x,y}}\geq\frac{1}{\mbox{{Rm}}}. $$

#### Corollary 3.4.

Under the hypotheses of Theorem 3.3, dynamo action requires that

$$ A_{2}\,\|\nabla_{x,y}\bm{u}^{\mathrm{A}}\|_{L^{\infty}_{z}L^{2}_{x,y}}\geq\frac{1}{\mbox{{Rm}}}. $$

In the plane layer, the magnetic field $\bm{B}$ decomposes into a poloidal component $\bm{B}^{\Phi}$ , a toroidal component $\bm{B}^{\Theta}$ , and a base flow component $\bm{B}^{0}$ . In particular,

$$ \bm{B}=\bm{B}^{\Phi}+\bm{B}^{\Theta}+\bm{B}^{0}. $$

The poloidal-toroidal (PT) decomposition, in particular its proper orthogonality and representation formulae for $\Phi$ and $\Theta$ , is reviewed in Appendix B. By design, it is a decomposition into orthogonal subspaces of $L^{2}_{\mathrm{sol}}$ on which the curl operator is chiral: if $\alpha\neq\beta\in\{\Phi,\Theta,0\}$ then

$$ \langle\bm{B}^{\alpha},\bm{B}^{\beta}\rangle=0,\qquad\langle\nabla\times\bm{B}^{\alpha},\nabla\times\bm{B}^{\beta}\rangle=0. $$

In the energy identity, the ohmic dissipation term then splits into poloidal-toroidal components. The magnetic energy production splits into interactions (Poisson brackets) of components in the PT decomposition. Estimating the interactions results in Theorem 3.3; the complete proof is given in Section 5.2.

#### Remark 3.2.

Unlike the Childress-type bounds, the three-dimensional Poincaré inequality is not used here. Instead, a two-dimensional Ladyzhenskaya inequality is applied on each horizontal surface.

### 3.2. Viscous Dynamo Theory

Inertialess dynamos in the plane layer have only been studied numerically with finite viscosity due to computational accessibility [CH17, HC16, HC19]. With finite viscosity $Ek>0$ , there is classical local regularity theory for the dynamo model (2.1): local-in-time smooth solutions exist for smooth initial conditions, Taylor’s constraint notwithstanding. Though the set of possible solutions is larger, it is not immediate that the threshold for dynamo action is lower–viscosity introduces dissipation into the dynamics.

Our quantitative antidynamo theory is robust to finite viscosity $Ek>0$ . Our condition in terms of the temperature holds with viscous corrections

#### Theorem 3.5.

Fix $\mbox{{Ek}}>0$ and consider the viscous inertialess model. Suppose that the magnetic flux is exact. Let $3\leq p\leq\infty$ and $0<\gamma<1$ . Then, for dynamo action it is necessary that

$$ \mbox{{Ra}}\,A_{p}\|\nabla_{x,y}\overline{T}\|_{L^{p}}+\mbox{{Ra}}^{2}\,\mbox{{Ek}}^{1-\gamma}\|\nabla\nabla_{x,y}\overline{T}\|^{2}_{L^{2}}\,\geq\frac{1}{\mbox{{Rm}}} $$

or

$$ 4\Lambda\int|\nabla\bm{B}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}V\leq\mbox{{Ek}}^{\gamma}. $$

The statement holds for any real number $\gamma$ . However, for $0<\gamma<1$ in particular the result is nontrivial in the inviscid limit: both exponents $\gamma$ and $1-\gamma$ are positive such that Theorem 3.1 is recovered as $\mbox{{Ek}}\to 0$ . Our refinement via the poloidal-toroidal decomposition holds with identical corrections for finite viscosity.

Our condition for dynamo action in terms of Archimedean fluid velocity holds also for the viscous inertialess model. For $\mbox{{Ek}}>0$ , the Archimedean fluid velocity $\bm{u}^{\mathrm{A}}$ is the solution to

$$ -\mbox{{Ek}}\nabla^{2}\bm{u}^{\mathrm{A}}+\bm{e}_{z}\times\bm{u}^{\mathrm{A}}+\nabla P^{\mathrm{A}}=\mbox{{Ra}}\,T\bm{e}_{z},\quad\nabla\cdot\bm{u}^{\mathrm{A}}=0, $$

subject to no-penetration and stress-free boundary conditions; $\bm{u}^{\mathrm{A}}$ is guaranteed to be unique and smooth for $\mbox{{Ek}}>0$ , with continuous dependence on $T$ .

#### Theorem 3.6.

Fix $\mbox{{Ek}}>0$ and consider the viscous inertialess model. Suppose that the magnetic flux is exact. Then, for dynamo action it is necessary that, for $3\leq p\leq\infty$ ,

$$ A_{p}\|\bm{u}^{\mathrm{A}}\|_{p}\geq\frac{1}{\mbox{{Rm}}}. $$

Our final result for the inertialess viscous model concerns the magnetohydrodynamic evolution of the electric current

$$ \bm{J}=\nabla\times\bm{B}. $$

Magnetic enstrophy $\int|\nabla\times\bm{B}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}V$ is the energy of the current, and is proportional to ohmic dissipation. Differentiating the induction equation (3.2c) results in

$$ \partial_{t}\bm{J}-\frac{1}{Rm}\nabla^{2}\bm{J}=\nabla(\nabla\cdot(\bm{u}\times\bm{B}))-\nabla^{2}(\bm{u}\times\bm{B}). $$

In the current energy identity, the gradient term vanishes because $\bm{J}$ is divergence-free. For ferromagnetic boundary conditions, sufficiently smooth solutions satisfy

$$ \frac{1}{2}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\int|\bm{J}|^{2}\mathrm{d}V+\frac{1}{Rm}\int|\nabla\bm{J}|^{2}\mathrm{d}V=-\int\bm{J}\cdot\nabla^{2}(\bm{u}\times\bm{B})\mathrm{d}V. $$

We identify a region of parameters in solution space where current dissipation necessarily dominates all mechanisms of (magnetic) enstrophy production.

#### Theorem 3.7.

Fix $\mbox{{Ek}}>0$ and consider the viscous inertialess model. Suppose that the magnetic flux is exact and that the temperature satisfies isothermal boundary conditions. Let $0<\gamma<1$ , and suppose that

$$ Rm<\frac{2Ek^{1-\gamma}}{C_{m}^{2}C_{\mathrm{P}}^{2}}. $$

Then, for magnetic enstrophy growth,

$$ \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(\frac{1}{2}\int|\bm{J}|^{2}\mathrm{d}V\right)\geq 0, $$

it is necessary that

$$ C_{n}\mbox{{Ra}}\,\|\overline{\nabla\times\nabla\times T\bm{e}_{z}}\|_{L^{2}}+Ra^{2}Ek^{1-\gamma}\|\nabla\times\overline{\nabla\times\nabla\times T\bm{e}_{z}}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\geq\frac{1}{2\mbox{{Rm}}}, $$

or it does not hold

$$ Ek^{\gamma}\leq 2\Lambda\int|\nabla\bm{J}|^{2}\mathrm{d}V\leq Ek^{\gamma}\left(\frac{4}{C_{m}^{2}C_{\mathrm{P}}^{2}}\frac{1}{RmEk^{\gamma-1}}-1\right). $$

The result relies on a nonlinear interaction between the ferromagnetic boundary conditions for $\bm{B}$ and the stress-free boundary conditions for $\bm{u}$ . In fact, the current $\bm{J}$ here satisfies an analogue of the stress-free condition.

#### Remark 3.3.

The smallness condition on Rm is used to control a fluid enstrophy term. If one forgoes this control, one can fix $\mbox{{Rm}}>0$ and take $\mbox{{Ek}}\to 0$ such that, in the inviscid limit, the first magnetic enstrophy growth requirement is

$$ C_{m}\|\nabla\bm{u}\|_{L^{2}}+C_{n}\mbox{{Ra}}\,\|\overline{\nabla\times\nabla\times T\bm{e}_{z}}\|_{L^{2}}\geq\frac{1}{\mbox{{Rm}}}. $$

#### Remark 3.4.

Limited enstrophy growth does not guarantee dynamo action.

The proofs of the results in this subsection are given in Section 6.

## 4. On Convection Driven Dynamo

In the preceding section, dynamo conditions are presented in terms of the modified Rayleigh number Ra and are independent of the model for temperature $T$ . In this section, we use the temperature equation to obtain constraints on the nondimensional parameters for sustained dynamo action.

To match the convection literature, the conditions here shall be reported in terms of “classical” Rayleigh numbers. Classical here refers to a Rayleigh number defined strictly as a ratio between heating and diffusion due to material properties. The modified Rayleigh number Ra contains the rotation rate, and for the case where we permit viscosity and $Ek>0$ , would be coupled to $Ek$ and so it is appropriate to separate the two.

In this section, we shall analyze coupling of the inertialess force balance with basic temperature dynamics. The temperature equation is

$$ \partial_{t}T+\nabla\cdot(\bm{u}T)=\frac{1}{\mbox{{Pe}}}\nabla^{2}T+\frac{Q}{\mbox{{Pe}}}. $$

Recall the Peclet number Pe measures the ratio of thermal advection to thermal diffusion. In the inviscid case $\mbox{{Ek}}=0$ , we report conditions for dynamo action for absorbing balls in the long-time dynamics of (4.1). In the viscous case, we report requirements for (instantaneous) dynamo action for small Pe.

### 4.1. Inviscid Case

In its long time dynamics, we identify an absorbing ball for the critical quantity necessary for (instantaneous) dynamo action. The radius of the absorbing ball is expressed in terms of the long-time quantity

$$ U_{\infty}=C_{\mathrm{S},0}\limsup_{t\to\infty}\|\bm{u}\|_{L^{3}}+C_{\infty}\limsup_{t\to\infty}\|\nabla\bm{u}\|_{2} $$

where $C_{\infty}$ and $C_{\mathrm{S},0}$ are positive constants from Sobolev embeddings.

#### Theorem 4.1.

Suppose $T$ satisfies the temperature equation and homoegenous isothermal boundary conditions. Suppose that $Q\in H^{1}$ is time independent and let

$$ U_{\infty}Pe<\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{1+\pi^{2}}}, $$

then,

$$ \limsup_{t\to\infty}\|\nabla_{x,y}\overline{T}(t)\|_{L^{3}}\leq R_{3}:=\frac{b_{3}\,C_{\mathrm{S}}^{1/2}\|Q\|^{1/4}_{2}}{\sqrt{\pi}}\left(\frac{U_{\infty}\mbox{{Pe}}\,\|Q\|_{H^{1}}}{\pi-\sqrt{1+\pi^{2}}U_{\infty}\mbox{{Pe}}}+\|Q\|_{2}\right)^{3/4}. $$

The results of §3.1 are stated without specifying a timescale and information from the temperature equation. We start by specifying a more classical Rayleigh number to separate the parameters responsible for heating from rotation in the inviscid and viscous problems. We define the nondimensional parameters:

$$ \begin{array}[]{r l}\text{Rayleigh:}&\mbox{{Ra}}_{\eta}=g\alpha T_{0}d^{3}/(\eta\kappa)\\
\text{magnetic Ekman:}&\mbox{{Ek}}_{\eta}=\eta/(2\Omega d^{2}).\end{array} $$

The relation to the parameters (2.7) is given by

$$ \mbox{{Ra}}_{\eta}\,Ek_{\eta}=\mbox{{Pe}}\,\mbox{{Ra}}. $$

Theorem 3.1, can be recast in terms of this more standard Rayleigh number $\mbox{{Ra}}_{\eta}$ which is independent of the rotation rate.

#### Corollary 4.2.

Consider the Taylor model, and fix a uniform heat source $Q=1.$ If $T$ is in the absorbing ball defined by Theorem 4.1, then dynamo action requires

$$ \mbox{{Ra}}_{\eta}\geq\frac{2^{4/3}\pi^{3/2}}{3\sqrt{3}C^{3/2}_{\mathrm{S}}b_{3}}\left(\frac{U_{\infty}\mbox{{Pe}}}{\pi-\sqrt{1+\pi^{2}}U_{\infty}\mbox{{Pe}}}+1\right)^{-3/4}\frac{1}{q\,\mbox{{Ek}}_{\eta}}. $$

#### Remark 4.1.

Formally, if $U_{\infty}\mbox{{Pe}}\ll 1$ then the requirement is

$$ \mbox{{Ra}}_{\eta}\geq\left(\frac{2^{4/3}\pi^{3/2}}{3\sqrt{3}C_{\mathrm{S}}^{3/2}b_{3}}\right)\frac{1}{q\,\mbox{{Ek}}_{\eta}}. $$

Next, we reinterpret the result from the poloidal-toroidal decomposition of the magnetic dissipation and Lorentz force presented in §3.1.2. In this case for the mix-norm we do not have to use Theorem 4.1. Instead, the critical quantity has a simpler absorption radius

#### Theorem 4.3.

Suppose $T$ satisfies the temperature equation and isothermal boundary conditions. Suppose that $Q\in H^{1}$ is time independent and let

$$ U_{\infty}Pe<\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{1+\pi^{2}}}, $$

then,

$$ \limsup_{t\to\infty}\|\nabla_{x,y}^{2}\overline{T}(t)\|_{L^{\infty}_{z}L^{2}_{x,y}}\leq R_{2}:=\left(\frac{U_{\infty}\mbox{{Pe}}\,\|Q\|_{H^{1}}}{\pi-\sqrt{1+\pi^{2}}U_{\infty}\mbox{{Pe}}}+\|Q\|_{L^{2}}\right). $$

#### Corollary 4.4.

Consider the Taylor model, and fix a uniform heat source $Q=1.$ If $T$ is in the absorbing ball defined by Theorem 4.3, then dynamo action requires

$$ \mbox{{Ra}}_{\eta}\geq\frac{C_{\mathrm{P}}^{1/2}}{C_{\mathrm{S}}^{3/2}}\left(\frac{U_{\infty}\mbox{{Pe}}}{\pi-\sqrt{1+\pi^{2}}U_{\infty}\mbox{{Pe}}}+1\right)^{-1}\frac{1}{q\,\mbox{{Ek}}_{\eta}}. $$

#### Remark 4.2.

Formally, if $U_{\infty}\mbox{{Pe}}\ll 1$ , the requirement is

$$ \mbox{{Ra}}_{\eta}\geq\left(\frac{C^{1/2}_{P}}{C_{\mathrm{S}}^{3/2}}\right)\frac{1}{q\,\mbox{{Ek}}_{\eta}}. $$

### 4.2. Viscous Case

For the viscous model, the classical Rayleigh $\mbox{{Ra}}_{\nu}$ number often used in studies of convection provides a natural decoupling of heating from the rotation rate. Explicitly

$$ \begin{array}[]{r l}\text{Rayleigh:}&\mbox{{Ra}}_{\nu}=g\alpha T_{0}d^{3}/(\nu\kappa)\end{array} $$

The relation to the parameter (2.7) is given by

$$ \mbox{{Ra}}_{\nu}\,Ek=\mbox{{Ra}}\,\mbox{{Pe}}. $$

In terms of the classical Rayleigh number, our constraint for (instantaneous) dynamo action has the alternative form

#### Theorem 4.5.

Fix $\mbox{{Ek}}>0$ and consider the viscous inertialess model. Suppose that the magnetic flux is exact. Then, for dynamo action it is necessary that, for $0<\gamma<1$ ,

$$ \mbox{{Ra}}_{\nu}\|\nabla^{2}T\|_{L^{2}}\geq\frac{A_{2}}{2C^{2}_{\mathrm{P},2}}\mbox{{Pe}}\,\mbox{{Ek}}^{-2+\gamma}\left(-1+\sqrt{1+\frac{4C^{2}_{\mathrm{P},2}\mbox{{Ek}}^{1-\gamma}}{A_{2}^{2}\mbox{{Rm}}}}\right). $$

#### Remark 4.3.

The choice $\gamma=\frac{1}{2}$ is natural, since in the original Theorem 3.5, both constraints tend to the inviscid limit at the same rate in $Ek$ . For $\delta>0$ , suppose that

$$ \mbox{{Rm}}\leq\frac{4C^{2}_{\mathrm{P},2}}{A_{2}^{2}(2+\delta)\delta}Ek^{1/2}, $$

then the requirement for dynamo action is

$$ Ra_{\nu}\|\nabla^{2}T\|_{L^{2}}\geq\frac{A_{2}\delta}{2C^{2}_{P,2}}Pe\,Ek^{-3/2}. $$

If (4.9) is an equality and since $Rm=q\,Pe$ , the requirement for dynamo action is

$$ Ra_{\nu}\|\nabla^{2}T\|_{2}\geq\frac{2}{A_{2}(2+\delta)}q^{-1}Ek^{-1}. $$

Note that these constraints are instantaneous and are independent of the dynamics of temperature $T$ . See §7.2 for the proof of theorem 4.5. A long-time prediction can be obtained by referring to the temperature equation and substituting the radius of the absorbing ball for $\|\nabla^{2}T\|_{2}$ identified in Proposition 7.2 into Theorem 4.5.

A significant feature is that the parameter $\mbox{{Ra}}_{\nu}$ has a critical value such that the conductive state of the system is linearly unstable. If $Q=Q(z)$ , the conductive state $\tau=\tau(z)$ is given by

$$ \tau^{\prime\prime}+Q=0,\qquad\tau\,|_{\,S_{\pm}}=T_{\pm}. $$

It is only perturbation about the conductive state $\theta=T-\tau$ which may drive dynamo action. Indeed, $\theta=0$ on the boundaries $S_{\pm}$ and it holds $\nabla_{x,y}\overline{\theta}=\nabla_{x,y}\overline{T}$ ; the magnetic energy production term has the form

$$ \int u_{z}T\,\mathrm{d}V=\int u_{z}\theta\,\mathrm{d}V. $$

#### Theorem 4.6.

Fix $\mbox{{Ek}}>0$ and consider the viscous inertialess model. Suppose that the magnetic flux is exact and let $\tau$ be the conductive state for heating $Q=Q(z)$ and $T_{\pm}$ . For non-trivial fields, combined energy growth,

$$ \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(\frac{\Lambda}{2}\int|\bm{B}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}V+\frac{\mbox{{Pe}}}{2}\int|\nabla\theta|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}V\right)\geq 0, $$

requires that, for $3\leq p\leq\infty$

$$ Ra\,A_{p}\,\|\nabla_{x,y}\overline{T}\|_{L^{p}}\geq\frac{1}{\mbox{{Rm}}}, $$

or it holds

$$ \frac{C_{\mathrm{P},2}\,Ra\sqrt{Ek}}{2}+\frac{\mbox{{Pe}}\,\|\tau^{\prime}\|_{L^{2}_{z}}}{2\sqrt{Ek}}\geq\sqrt{1-\mbox{{Pe}}\,C_{\mathrm{S},0}\|\bm{u}\|_{L^{3}}}, $$

provided $PeC_{S,0}\|\bm{u}\|_{L^{3}}<1$ .

See §7.2 for a proof of Theorem 4.6.

#### Remark 4.4.

Formally, if $\|\bm{u}\|_{L^{3}}\mbox{{Pe}}\ll 1$ , the second requirement is

$$ C_{\mathrm{P},2}\,Ra\sqrt{Ek}+\frac{\mbox{{Pe}}\,\|\tau^{\prime}\|_{L^{2}_{z}}}{\sqrt{Ek}}\geq 2. $$

Notably, in the case of small Pe, combined energy growth is essentially dynamo action. In terms of the classical Rayleigh number $\mbox{{Ra}}_{\nu}$ defined in (4.7), the condition for energy growth (4.14) at small Pe is

$$ \frac{C_{\mathrm{P},2}\,Ra_{\nu}\,Ek^{3/2}}{Pe}+\frac{Pe\|\tau^{\prime}\|_{L^{2}_{z}}}{\sqrt{Ek}}\geq 2. $$

Let us consider formal asymptotics for small Pe in the inviscid limit. If we posit $Pe\sim Ek^{n}$ , then up to independent constants the above expression becomes

$$ Ra_{\nu}\gtrsim Ek^{-1}(Ek^{n-\frac{1}{2}}-\|\tau^{\prime}\|_{2}Ek^{2n-1}). $$

If $\frac{1}{2}<n<\frac{3}{2}$ , both exponents $n-\frac{1}{2}$ and $2n-1$ are positive; thus in the inviscid limit $\mbox{{Ek}}\to 0$ , the requirement (4.16) imposes a nontrivial restriction for combined energy growth, i.e., dynamo action. In particular, one has $\mbox{{Ra}}_{\nu}\gtrsim\mbox{{Ek}}^{n-3/2}$ . In the critical case, $n=\frac{1}{2}$ , the asymptotic restriction is $Ra_{\nu}\gtrsim Ek^{-1}(1-\|\tau^{\prime}\|_{2})$ .

#### Remark 4.5.

One can predict a scaling of $Ek^{-3/2}$ for $\mbox{{Ra}}_{\nu}$ without an asymptotic restriction on $Pe>0$ . If $\|\tau^{\prime}\|_{L^{2}_{z}}\mbox{{Ek}}^{-1/2}\ll 1$ , then the condition in Theorem 4.6 is

$$ Ra_{\nu}\gtrsim Ek^{-3/2}Pe(1-C_{\mathrm{S},0}Pe\|\bm{u}\|_{L^{3}})^{1/2}. $$

Sufficiently oscillatory or concentrated $Q$ satisfy this condition. Explicit examples are $Q(z)=\sin(\pi z/Ek^{1/2+\epsilon})$ or $Q(z)=\bm{1}_{[0,Ek^{1+\epsilon}]}Ek^{-(1+\epsilon)}$ for any $\epsilon>0$ .

## 5. Proof of Theorems: Inviscid Case

Our antidynamo Theorems rely on functional identities, decompositions and inequalities. The analysis begins with the fact that our governing equations admits a basic (magnetic) energy identity

#### Lemma 5.1 (Magnetic Energy Balance).

Consider the Taylor model (3.2) and suppose that the nondimensional parameters are all finite. Then for a smooth solution,

$$ \frac{1}{2}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\int|\bm{B}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}V+\frac{1}{\mbox{{Rm}}}\int|\nabla\bm{B}|^{2}\mathrm{d}V=\frac{Ra}{\Lambda}\int u_{z}T\mathrm{d}V. $$

#### Proof.

Applying $\langle\bm{B},\cdot\,\rangle$ to the induction equation (3.2c) and integrating by parts results in

$$ \frac{1}{2}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\int|\bm{B}|^{2}\mathrm{d}V+\frac{1}{\mbox{{Rm}}}\int|\nabla\bm{B}|^{2}\mathrm{d}V=\langle\bm{u},\bm{B}\times(\nabla\times\bm{B})\rangle. $$

Indeed, integrating by parts the ohmic dissipation term yields

$$ \langle\bm{B},\nabla^{2}\bm{B}\rangle+\int\bm{n}_{\pm}\cdot(\nabla\times\bm{B})\times\bm{B}\,\mathrm{d}S_{\pm}=-\int|\nabla\bm{B}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}V, $$

and the boundary term vanishes because (3.3b) implies $\bm{B}$ is normal to the boundary. Integrating by parts the production term yields

$$ \langle\bm{B},\nabla\times(\bm{u}\times\bm{B})\rangle+\int\bm{n}_{\pm}\cdot\bm{B}\times(\bm{u}\times\bm{B})\,\mathrm{d}{S_{\pm}}=\langle\bm{u},\bm{B}\times(\nabla\times\bm{B})\rangle. $$

and the boundary term vanishes because (3.3a) implies $\bm{u}$ is tangent to the boundary.

Applying $\langle\bm{u},\cdot\,\rangle$ to the momentum equation (3.2a) results in

$$ \langle\bm{u},\bm{B}\times(\nabla\times\bm{B})\rangle=\frac{Ra}{\Lambda}\int u_{z}T\mathrm{d}V. $$

Substituting (5.4) into (5.1) produces the desired identity. ∎

### 5.1. Childress-type Bounds

#### Proof of Theorem 3.1.

The curl of the momentum equation is

$$ -\partial_{z}\bm{u}=\Lambda\,\nabla\times\bm{F}^{\mathrm{M}}-\mbox{{Ra}}\,\bm{e}_{z}\times\nabla T, $$

where we recall the notation

$$ \bm{F}^{\mathrm{M}}=(\nabla\times\bm{B})\times\bm{B}. $$

Integrating by parts in $\mathrm{d}z$

$$ \displaystyle\int u_{z}T\,\mathrm{d}V \displaystyle=-\int\partial_{z}u_{z}\left(\int_{0}^{z}T(x,y,z^{\prime})\,\mathrm{d}z^{\prime}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}z, $$

the boundary terms vanished because $u_{z}=0$ on the boundaries. Therefore, after substituting (5.5), we have the expression

$$ \int u_{z}T\,\mathrm{d}V=-\langle\partial_{z}\bm{u},\overline{T}\bm{e}_{z}\rangle=\Lambda\langle\nabla\times\bm{F}^{\mathrm{M}},\overline{T}\bm{e}_{z}\rangle. $$

Integrating by parts the right hands side yields

$$ \langle\nabla\times\bm{F}^{\mathrm{M}},\overline{T}\bm{e}_{z}\rangle+\int\bm{n}_{\pm}\cdot\bm{F}^{\mathrm{M}}\times\overline{T}\bm{e}_{z}\,\mathrm{d}S_{\pm}=-\langle\bm{F}^{\mathrm{M}},\bm{e}_{z}\times\nabla\overline{T}\rangle, $$

where the boundary term vanishes. Observe, we have simply integrated by parts the perpendicular horizontal gradient

$$ \bm{e}_{z}\times\nabla f=-\partial_{y}f\bm{e}_{x}+\partial_{x}f\bm{e}_{y}=\nabla^{\perp}_{x,y}f. $$

Substituting (5.9) into the expression (5.8), we discover a new identity for the production of magnetic energy

$$ \frac{\mbox{{Ra}}}{\Lambda}\int Tu_{z}\,\mathrm{d}V=-\mbox{{Ra}}\int\nabla^{\perp}_{x,y}\overline{T}\cdot(\nabla\times\bm{B})\times\bm{B}\,\mathrm{d}V. $$

To conclude, we require

#### Lemma 5.2.

Let a magnetic field $\bm{B}$ satisfy ferromagnetic boundary conditions and

$$ \int\bm{n}_{\pm}\cdot\bm{B}\,\mathrm{d}S_{\pm}=0. $$

Then for $3\leq p\leq\infty$ there is a constant $A_{p}$ such that it holds

$$ \left|\int\bm{v}\cdot(\nabla\times\bm{B})\times\bm{B}\,\mathrm{d}V\right|\leq A_{p}\|\bm{v}\|_{L^{p}}\int|\nabla\bm{B}|^{2}\mathrm{d}V. $$

Applying Lemma 5.2 yields

$$ \displaystyle\mbox{{Ra}}\int\nabla^{\perp}_{x,y}\overline{T}\cdot(\nabla\times\bm{B})\times\bm{B}\,\mathrm{d}V- \displaystyle\frac{1}{\mbox{{Rm}}}\int|\nabla\bm{B}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}V \displaystyle\leq\left(A_{p}\mbox{{Ra}}\,\|\nabla_{x,y}\overline{T}\|_{L^{p}}-\frac{1}{\mbox{{Rm}}}\right)\int|\nabla\bm{B}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}V. $$

By Lemma 5.1, our identity (5.11) and estimate (5.12), we have thus established

$$ \frac{1}{2}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\int|\bm{B}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}V\leq\left(A_{p}\mbox{{Ra}}\,\|\nabla_{x,y}\overline{T}\|_{L^{p}}-\frac{1}{\mbox{{Rm}}}\right)\int|\nabla\bm{B}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}V. $$

Dynamo action therefore requires that the expression in the parentheses above is nonnegative. ∎

#### Proof of Lemma 5.2.

By Hölder’s inequality with exponents

$$ \frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{r}=\frac{1}{2}, $$

it holds

$$ \int\bm{v}\cdot(\nabla\times\bm{B})\times\bm{B}\,\mathrm{d}V\leq\|\bm{v}\|_{L^{p}}\|\bm{B}\|_{L^{r}}\|\nabla\times\bm{B}\|_{L^{2}}. $$

Because $3\leq p\leq\infty$ , it follows that $2\leq r\leq 6$ are the endpoints. We then bound $L^{r}$ by an interpolation of the endpoint norms

$$ \|\bm{B}\|_{L^{r}}\leq\|\bm{B}\|^{\frac{6-r}{2r}}_{L^{2}}\|\bm{B}\|^{\frac{3r-6}{2r}}_{L^{6}}. $$

With ferromagnetic boundary conditions, the kernel of the curl operator in the space of solenoidal vector fields are exactly constant vectors in the $z$ direction. Because we assumed $\int B_{z}\,\mathrm{d}S_{\pm}=0$ , these constant vectors must be zero in our case and the kernel is trivial. Therefore, from the Poincaré inequality it holds

$$ \|\bm{B}\|_{L^{2}}\leq C_{\mathrm{P}}\|\nabla\times\bm{B}\|_{L^{2}}, $$

and from the Sobolev embedding it holds

$$ \|\bm{B}\|_{L^{6}}\leq C_{\mathrm{S}}\|\nabla\times\bm{B}\|_{L^{2}}. $$

Combining (5.17) and (5.18) with (5.16), we have established that

$$ \|\bm{B}\|_{L^{r}}\leq C_{\mathrm{P}}^{\frac{6-r}{2r}}C_{\mathrm{S}}^{\frac{3r-6}{2r}}\|\nabla\times\bm{B}\|_{L^{2}}. $$

From the boundary conditions on $\bm{B}$ we have that $\|\nabla\times\bm{B}\|_{2}=\|\nabla\bm{B}\|_{2}$ . Applying (5.19) to (5.15), we have proven the claim for the constant

$$ A_{p}=C_{\mathrm{P}}^{\frac{p-3}{p}}C_{\mathrm{S}}^{\frac{3}{p}}. $$

∎

#### Proof of Theorem 3.2.

Taylor’s constraint implies

$$ \frac{\mbox{{Ra}}}{\Lambda}\langle\bm{u},\bm{F}^{\mathrm{A}}\rangle=\frac{\mbox{{Ra}}}{\Lambda}\langle\bm{u}^{\mathrm{M}},\bm{F}^{\mathrm{A}}\rangle=\frac{1}{\Lambda}\langle\bm{u}^{\mathrm{M}},\bm{e}_{z}\times\bm{u}^{\mathrm{A}}\rangle=-\langle\bm{u}^{\mathrm{A}},\bm{F}^{\mathrm{M}}\rangle. $$

The first equality follows from the no work properties (2.26) and (2.27) derived from the skew-symmetry of the Coriolis operator. The penultimate and last equality follow from equations (2.21) and (2.22).

We have discovered an identity for the production of magnetic energy

$$ \frac{\mbox{{Ra}}}{\Lambda}\int Tu_{z}\,\mathrm{d}V=-\int\bm{u}^{\mathrm{A}}\cdot(\nabla\times\bm{B})\times\bm{B}\,\mathrm{d}V. $$

Lemma 5.1 and Lemma 5.2 then imply

$$ \frac{1}{2}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\int|\bm{B}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}V\leq\left(A_{p}\,\|\bm{u}^{\mathrm{A}}\|_{L^{p}}-\frac{1}{\mbox{{Rm}}}\right)\int|\nabla\bm{B}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}V. $$

Therefore, dynamo action requires that the expression in the parentheses above is nonnegative. ∎

### 5.2. Poloidal-Toroidal Decomposition

The basic properties and representation formula for the PT decomposition are reviewed in Appendix B. In particular, any magnetic field in the plane layer is given by

$$ \bm{B}=\sum_{\alpha\in\{\Phi,\Theta,0\}}\bm{B}^{\alpha}, $$

where the poloidal and toroidal parts are

$$ \bm{B}^{\Phi}=\nabla\times\nabla\times\Phi\bm{e}_{z},\qquad\bm{B}^{\Theta}=\nabla\times\Theta\bm{e}_{z}, $$

and the base flow is

$$ \bm{B}^{0}=B^{0}_{x}(z)\,\bm{e}_{x}+B^{0}_{y}(z)\,\bm{e}_{y}. $$

The poloidal potential $\Phi$ , toroidal potential $\Theta$ and the horizontal base flow $\bm{B}^{0}$ have explicit representations.

#### Proof of Theorem 3.3.

Because for $\alpha\neq\beta$

$$ \displaystyle\left|\int\nabla\vartheta\cdot\nabla(\bm{u}\cdot\nabla T)\mathrm{d}V\right| \displaystyle\leq(\|\bm{u}\|_{L^{3}}\|\nabla\nabla T\|_{L^{6}}+\|\nabla\bm{u}\|_{L^{2}}\|\nabla T\|_{L^{\infty}})\|\nabla\vartheta\|_{L^{2}} $$

Next, given that $C_{\infty}$ and $C_{\mathrm{S}}$ be admissible Sobolev–elliptic constants satisfying

$$ \|\nabla T\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq C_{\infty}\|\nabla^{2}T\|_{H^{1}},\qquad\|\nabla\nabla T\|_{L^{6}}\leq C_{\mathrm{S},0}\|\nabla^{2}T\|_{H^{1}}. $$

Thus (7.11) and (7.12) motivate the definition (4.2) such that

$$ \left|\int\nabla\vartheta\cdot\nabla(\bm{u}\cdot\nabla T)\mathrm{d}V\right|\leq U_{\infty}\|\nabla^{2}T\|_{H^{1}}\|\nabla\vartheta\|_{L^{2}}. $$

On the other hand, by applying the Poincaré inequality to the definition of $\vartheta$ ,

$$ \|\nabla^{2}T\|_{H^{1}}\leq\left(1+\frac{1}{\pi^{2}}\right)^{1/2}\|\nabla\vartheta\|_{L^{2}}+\|Q\|_{H^{1}}. $$

Therefore, from (7.13),

$$ \left|\int\nabla\vartheta\cdot\nabla(\bm{u}\cdot\nabla T)\mathrm{d}V\right|\leq\left(1+\frac{1}{\pi^{2}}\right)^{1/2}U_{\infty}\|\nabla\vartheta\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+U_{\infty}\|Q\|_{H^{1}}\|\nabla\vartheta\|_{L^{2}}. $$

Combining (7.9) and (7.15) yields

$$ \frac{1}{2}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\|\vartheta\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\leq-\gamma\|\nabla\vartheta\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+U_{\infty}\|Q\|_{H^{1}}\|\nabla\vartheta\|_{L^{2}}. $$

where

$$ \gamma=\frac{1}{\mbox{{Pe}}}-\left(1+\frac{1}{\pi^{2}}\right)^{1/2}U_{\infty} $$

For any $\varepsilon>0$ , Young’s inequality gives

$$ U_{\infty}\|Q\|_{H^{1}}\|\nabla\vartheta\|_{L^{2}}\leq\varepsilon\gamma\|\nabla\vartheta\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\frac{U_{\infty}^{2}\|Q\|_{H^{1}}^{2}}{4\varepsilon\gamma}. $$

Substituting (7.18) into (7.16) with $\varepsilon=1/2$ gives

$$ \frac{1}{2}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\|\vartheta\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\leq-\frac{1}{2}\gamma\|\nabla\vartheta\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\frac{U_{\infty}^{2}\|Q\|_{H^{1}}^{2}}{2\gamma}. $$

Using Poincaré’s inequality again,

$$ \|\nabla\vartheta\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\geq\pi^{2}\|\vartheta\|_{L^{2}}^{2}, $$

we obtain

$$ \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\|\vartheta\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\leq-\gamma\pi^{2}\|\vartheta\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\frac{U_{\infty}^{2}\|Q\|_{H^{1}}^{2}}{\gamma}. $$

Gronwall’s inequality gives

$$ \displaystyle\|\vartheta(t)\|_{2}^{2} \displaystyle\leq\|\vartheta_{0}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\exp\{-\gamma\pi^{2}t\}+\frac{U_{\infty}^{2}\|Q\|_{H^{1}}^{2}}{\gamma^{2}\pi^{2}}\left(1-\exp\{-\gamma\pi^{2}t\}\right). $$

Therefore,

$$ \limsup_{t\to\infty}\|\vartheta(t)\|_{L^{2}}\leq\frac{U_{\infty}\|Q\|_{H^{1}}}{\gamma\pi}. $$

Finally, we have

$$ \|\nabla^{2}T\|_{L^{2}}\leq\|\vartheta\|_{L^{2}}+\|Q\|_{L^{2}}. $$

Combining (7.23) and (7.24) gives

$$ \limsup_{t\to\infty}\|\nabla^{2}T(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\leq\left(\frac{U_{\infty}\|Q\|_{H^{1}}}{\gamma\pi}+\|Q\|_{L^{2}}\right)^{2}. $$

This proves the result. ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 4.1.

In fact

$$ \|\nabla_{x,y}\overline{T}\|_{L^{3}}=\|\overline{\nabla_{x,y}T}\|_{L^{3}}\leq b_{3}\|\nabla_{x,y}T\|_{L^{3}}\leq b_{3}\|\nabla T\|_{L^{3}} $$

where $b_{3}$ is the constant given in Lemma 7.3. Then, by $L^{p}$ interpolation we have that

$$ \|\nabla T\|_{L^{3}}\leq\|\nabla T\|_{L^{2}}^{1/2}\|\nabla T\|_{L^{6}}^{1/2}. $$

Then, using the temperature boundary conditions, we can integrate by parts and use the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality to write that

$$ \int|\nabla T|^{2}\mathrm{d}V=-\int T\nabla^{2}T\mathrm{d}V\leq\|T\|_{L^{2}}\|\nabla^{2}T\|_{L^{2}}. $$

Using (7.28) and the Sobolev embedding $H^{1}\hookrightarrow L^{6}$ gives that

Taking long-time limit, we have that

$$ \|T\|_{L^{2}}\|\nabla^{2}T\|_{L^{2}}\leq\limsup_{t\to\infty}\left(\|T\|_{L^{2}}\|\nabla^{2}T\|_{L^{2}}\right)\leq\left(\limsup_{t\to\infty}\|T\|_{L^{2}}\right)\left(\limsup_{t\to\infty}\|\nabla^{2}T\|_{L^{2}}\right). $$

#### Proof of Theorem 4.3.

We shall establish

$$ \|\nabla_{x,y}^{2}\overline{T}\|_{L^{\infty}_{z}L^{2}_{x,y}}\leq\|\nabla^{2}T\|_{L^{2}} $$

and the claim follows from an application of Proposition 7.2.

A basic property of the integral is

$$ \left\|\int_{0}^{z}\nabla_{x,y}^{2}T(z^{\prime})\,dz^{\prime}\right\|_{L^{2}_{x,y}}\leq\int_{0}^{z}\|\nabla_{x,y}^{2}T(z^{\prime})\|_{L^{2}_{x,y}}dz^{\prime}. $$

Taking the supremum in $z$ , it holds

$$ \|\nabla_{x,y}^{2}\overline{T}\|_{L^{\infty}_{z}L^{2}_{x,y}}\leq\|\nabla_{x,y}^{2}T\|_{L^{2}}. $$

Now we establish

$$ \|\nabla_{x,y}^{2}T\|_{L^{2}}\leq\|\nabla^{2}T\|_{L^{2}}. $$

Observe that

$$ \langle\nabla^{2}T,\nabla^{2}T\rangle=\langle\nabla_{x,y}^{2}T,\nabla_{x,y}^{2}T\rangle+2\langle\partial_{z}^{2}T,\nabla_{x,y}^{2}T\rangle+\langle\partial_{z}^{2}T,\partial_{z}^{2}T\rangle. $$

The cross term we may integrate by parts in $dz$ ,

$$ \langle\partial_{z}^{2}T,\nabla_{x,y}^{2}T\rangle=-\langle\partial_{z}T,\nabla_{x,y}^{2}\partial_{z}T\rangle\pm\int(\partial_{z}T)\nabla_{x,y}^{2}T\,dS_{\pm}. $$

For isothermal boundary conditions $\nabla_{x,y}^{2}T$ vanishes on the boundary $S_{\pm}$ . Therefore we may further integrate by parts the cross term in $\mathrm{d}S$ such that

$$ \langle\partial_{z}^{2}T,\nabla_{x,y}^{2}T\rangle=\langle\nabla_{x,y}\partial_{z}T,T\partial_{z}T\rangle\geq 0. $$

This establishes estimate (7.34), and the result follows. ∎

Let $1\leq p<\infty$ and $\bm{f}\in L^{p}(\mathrm{d}V)$ . Then,

$$ \|\overline{f}\|_{L^{p}}\leq b_{p}\|f\|_{L^{p}}, $$

where

## 8. Discussion

This work establishes necessary conditions for the instantaneous growth of magnetic energy in rotating convection. We consider the magnetohydrodynamic model of J. B. Taylor for the Earth’s outer core, and its viscous extension. We prove antidynamo theorems: quantitative conditions that are necessary for magnetic energy growth in rapidly rotating convection. Our analysis identifies the horizontal variation of the vertically integrated temperature as the quantity controlling the necessary conditions for dynamo action. The bounds therefore extend the logic of classical kinematic antidynamo estimates to a fully nonlinear setting.

A finding of our work is the significance of the Archimedean velocity $\bm{u}^{\mathrm{A}}$ , i.e., the buoyancy-driven part of the flow. In particular, magnetic energy growth requires, for $3\leq p\leq\infty$

$$ \mbox{{Rm}}\,A_{p}\|\bm{u}^{\mathrm{A}}\|_{L^{p}}\geq 1, $$

where $A_{p}$ is an explicit constant given in Appendix A. The constraint holds for Taylor’s model and for the inertialess model with finite viscosity $\mbox{{Ek}}>0$ . The precise statements are Theorems 3.2 and 3.6. We refine our bound via poloidal-toroidal decomposition to replace $L^{p}$ with $L^{\infty}_{z}\dot{H}^{1}_{x,y}$ in the above constraint.

### 8.1. Taylor Dynamo

Taylor’s constraint complicates the analysis of the inertialess model. The production of magnetic energy in its basic form depends on the vertical (poloidal) component of the flow $u_{z}$ ; however, by identities from Taylor’s constraint, the magnetic energy production is driven by a purely horizontal (toroidal) part of the flow

$$ \bm{u}^{\mathrm{A}}=\mbox{{Ra}}\,\nabla_{x,y}^{\perp}\overline{T}. $$

Crucially, our results are independent of the geostrophic component of the flow which is typically difficult to compute. The precise statement is Theorem 3.1.

Our analysis without nondimensionalising yields the requirement for dynamo action

$$ \mbox{{Ra}}_{T}=\frac{g\alpha d^{1-\frac{3}{p}}\|\nabla_{x,y}\overline{T}\|_{L^{p}}}{2\Omega\eta}\geq A^{-1}_{p}. $$

Therefore, for flows normalised by the temperature scale given by a ( dimensional) $\|\nabla_{x,y}\overline{T}\|_{L^{p}}$ , a lower bound for Ra is $A^{-1}_{p}$ . In terms of a classical Rayleigh number $\mbox{{Ra}}_{\eta}$ our constraint for dynamo action has the form

$$ Ra_{\eta}\gtrsim q^{-1}Ek_{\eta}^{-1}. $$

In long-time convection, the implicit constant in this requirement depends on the radii of absorbing balls. For uniform internal heating, see Corollaries 4.2 and 4.4.

### 8.2. Viscous Dynamo

At finite Ekman number $\mbox{{Ek}}>0$ , viscosity removes the computational difficulties associated with the inviscid model. Our requirements for dynamo action hold with viscous corrections which vanish as $\mbox{{Ek}}\to 0$ ; our dynamo criteria are not based on singular properties of Taylor’s constraint.

The viscous corrections are explicitly given in Theorem 3.5. Writing Theorem 3.5 in terms of a classical Rayleigh number $Ra_{\nu}$ , our requirement for dynamo action takes the form

$$ Ra_{\nu}\gtrsim PeEk^{-3/2}. $$

In addition to the magnetic energy, in Theorem 3.7 we provide a necessary condition for the growth of magnetic enstrophy, given Rm is sufficiently small. The magnetic energy and enstrophy growth conditions are complementary. If growth conditions of magnetic energy enstrophy are both not satisfied, then the magnetic field and its gradients must decay.

Our final result concerns the thermo-magnetic energy $\mathcal{E}=\Lambda\|\bm{B}\|_{2}^{2}+Pe\|\nabla\theta\|_{2}^{2}$ in Theorem 4.6. The conductive profile affects the second combined energy condition through $\|\tau^{\prime}\|_{L^{2}_{z}}$ , where the conductive state corresponds to $Q(z)=-\tau^{\prime\prime}(z)$ . For the combined energy to grow, at least one of two conditions must be satisfied. The first is the magnetic energy condition of Theorem 3.6. The second result arises from a balance of thermal diffusion against the advection of thermal gradients, the conductive gradient $\tau^{\prime}$ and the viscous dissipation. In the case of $Pe\sim Ek^{1/2}$ for $Ek\ll 1$ where $\mathcal{E}\to\Lambda\|\bm{B}\|^{2}_{2}$ and non-decay requires $Ra_{\nu}\gtrsim Ek^{-1}$ . For $Pe\sim 1$ and conductive states such that $\|\tau^{\prime}\|_{L^{2}_{z}}\mbox{{Ek}}^{-1/2}\ll 1$ , the non-decay requirement is $Ra_{\nu}\gtrsim Ek^{-3/2}$ as before. Such conductive states are generated by heating profiles $Q=Q(z)$ which are oscillatory or concentrated at the boundaries.

In particular, there exists a critical Rayleigh number $Ra_{\nu}^{*}$ , above which the flow is linearly unstable to convection. ### 8.3. Scope and Future Outlook

Several qualifications should be kept in mind when interpreting these results. First, our conditions are strictly necessary, but are not sufficient for dynamo action. A smooth solution to the inertialess models may continuously satisfy our constraints without exhibiting any magnetic energy growth. We impose strictly impenetrable, stress-free and ferromagnetic boundary conditions however several of our arguments apply to spherical domains, mutatis mutandis.

The numerical values of the thresholds use admissible rather than sharp constants (appendix A). The constants depend on the domain. The temperature absorbing radii introduce additional losses when the entire temperature gradient is estimated instead of its dynamically relevant horizontal structures. The bounds should consequently be regarded as quantitative but conservative. The results in section 3 can be applied to different equations governing the temperature, provided the buoyancy force retains the same structure. As such the results can apply to double-diffusive convection [HT81, Gar18]. An interesting application would be to alternative models like Maxwell-Cattaneo convection [HPE21], convection with anisotropic or nonlinear thermal diffusion, or anelastic convection [AJS05].

It would be useful to evaluate the necessary conditions using numerical dynamo solutions, both to measure the gap between the inequalities and observed onset and to identify which estimates produce the largest losses [JR00, HC16, CH17, HC19]. Finally, the study of magnetohydrodynamics with recent mathematical tools would be valuable, like methods for bounding the long-time averages of quantities, used to study turbulence [FAW22]. Establishing such long-time constraints would turn the instantaneous obstructions derived here into a nonlinear analogue of the classical antidynamo theory for sustained magnetic fields.

#### Proof of $C_{\mathrm{S}}$ .

Let $\bm{B}$ be horizontally periodic, solenoidal, and satisfy ferromagnetic boundary conditions in addition to net zero flux. Then the constant $C_{\mathrm{S}}$ appears in the inequality $\|\bm{B}\|_{L^{6}(V)}\leq C_{\mathrm{S}}\|\nabla\bm{B}\|_{L^{2}(V)}$ where $V=[0,L_{x}]\times[0,L_{y}]\times[0,1]$ .

We construct an extension to which the whole-space Sobolev inequality can be applied. Extend $B_{x}$ and $B_{y}$ oddly across $z=0,1$ , extend $B_{z}$ evenly across these planes, and extend all three components periodically in $x$ and $y$ . Denote the resulting field by $\widetilde{\bm{B}}$ . The boundary conditions ensure that $\widetilde{\bm{B}}\in H^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$ .

Consider the enlarged box

$$ W=(-L_{x},2L_{x})\times(-L_{y},2L_{y})\times(-1,2). $$

Choose a product cutoff

$$ \eta(x,y,z)=\eta_{x}(x)\eta_{y}(y)\eta_{z}(z) $$

such that $\eta=1$ on $V$ , $\eta=0$ on $\partial W$ , and each factor varies linearly across the two adjoining cells.

To estimate the cutoff more precisely, set

$$ \ell_{x}=L_{x},\qquad\ell_{y}=L_{y},\qquad\ell_{z}=1. $$

For $i\in\{x,y,z\}$ and $s\in[0,\ell_{i}]$ , the three values of the corresponding cutoff factor satisfy

$$ \displaystyle\eta_{i}(s-\ell_{i}) \displaystyle=\frac{s}{\ell_{i}}, \displaystyle\eta_{i}(s) \displaystyle=1, \displaystyle\eta_{i}(s+\ell_{i}) \displaystyle=1-\frac{s}{\ell_{i}}. $$

Consequently,

$$ \sum_{j=-1}^{1}\eta_{i}(s+j\ell_{i})^{2}=1+\left(\frac{s}{\ell_{i}}\right)^{2}+\left(1-\frac{s}{\ell_{i}}\right)^{2}\leq 2, $$

and

$$ \sum_{j=-1}^{1}\left|\eta_{i}^{\prime}(s+j\ell_{i})\right|^{2}=\frac{2}{\ell_{i}^{2}}. $$

Set

$$ \bm{F}=\eta\widetilde{\bm{B}} $$

on $W$ , and extend $\bm{F}$ by zero outside $W$ . Then $\bm{F}\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{3};\mathbb{R}^{3})$ and $\bm{F}=\bm{B}$ on $V$ . By the product rule,

$$ \nabla\bm{F}=\eta\nabla\widetilde{\bm{B}}+\widetilde{\bm{B}}\otimes\nabla\eta. $$

Decomposing $W$ into its $27$ translated and reflected copies of $V$ , and using (A.4) in each coordinate, gives

$$ \displaystyle\|\eta\nabla\widetilde{\bm{B}}\|_{L^{2}(W)}^{2} \displaystyle\leq 2^{3}\|\nabla\bm{B}\|_{L^{2}(V)}^{2} \displaystyle=8\|\nabla\bm{B}\|_{L^{2}(V)}^{2}. $$

Hence,

$$ \|\eta\nabla\widetilde{\bm{B}}\|_{L^{2}(W)}\leq 2\sqrt{2}\,\|\nabla\bm{B}\|_{L^{2}(V)}. $$

Similarly, since

$$ \displaystyle|\nabla\eta|^{2}={} \displaystyle|\eta_{x}^{\prime}|^{2}\eta_{y}^{2}\eta_{z}^{2}+\eta_{x}^{2}|\eta_{y}^{\prime}|^{2}\eta_{z}^{2} \displaystyle+\eta_{x}^{2}\eta_{y}^{2}|\eta_{z}^{\prime}|^{2}, $$

equations (A.4) and (A.5) imply

$$ \displaystyle\|\widetilde{\bm{B}}\otimes\nabla\eta\|_{L^{2}(W)}^{2}\leq{} \displaystyle 8\left(L_{x}^{-2}+L_{y}^{-2}+1\right)\|\bm{B}\|_{L^{2}(V)}^{2}. $$

Therefore,

$$ \|\widetilde{\bm{B}}\otimes\nabla\eta\|_{L^{2}(W)}\leq 2\sqrt{2}\,\sqrt{1+L_{x}^{-2}+L_{y}^{-2}}\,\|\bm{B}\|_{L^{2}(V)}. $$

Combining (A.6), (A.8), and (A.10), we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\|\nabla\bm{F}\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3})}\leq 2\sqrt{2}\Bigl(\|\nabla\bm{B}\|_{L^{2}(V)} \displaystyle+\sqrt{1+L_{x}^{-2}+L_{y}^{-2}}\,\|\bm{B}\|_{L^{2}(V)}\Bigr). $$

Using the Poincaré inequality then gives

$$ \displaystyle\|\nabla\bm{F}\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3})}\leq 2\sqrt{2}\left(1+\frac{\sqrt{1+L_{x}^{-2}+L_{y}^{-2}}}{\lambda_{1}}\right)\|\nabla\bm{B}\|_{L^{2}(V)}. $$

Talenti’s sharp whole-space Sobolev inequality, applied to $|\bm{F}|$ , gives

$$ \|\bm{F}\|_{L^{6}(\mathbb{R}^{3})}\leq C_{3}\|\nabla|\bm{F}|\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3})}\leq C_{3}\|\nabla\bm{F}\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3})}. $$

Since $\bm{F}=\bm{B}$ on $V$ , it follows from (A.12) that

$$ \|\bm{B}\|_{L^{6}(V)}\leq C_{\mathrm{S}}\|\nabla\bm{B}\|_{L^{2}(V)}, $$

with

$$ C_{\mathrm{S}}=2\sqrt{2}\,C_{3}\left(1+\frac{\sqrt{1+L_{x}^{-2}+L_{y}^{-2}}}{\lambda_{1}}\right). $$

∎

#### Remark A.1.

If a scalar or vector $f$ admits an $H^{1}_{loc}$ reflected extension to the enlarged domain and satisfies $\|f\|_{2}\leq\frac{1}{\lambda_{1}}\|\nabla f\|_{2}$ then the cutoff calculation proves $\|f\|_{6}\leq C_{6}\|\nabla f\|_{2}$ .

#### Remark A.2.

If a Poincaré inequality does not exist, as for the case of $\nabla^{2}T$ , then

$$ \|F\|_{6}\leq C_{\mathrm{S},0}\|F\|_{H^{1}} $$

where

$$ C_{\mathrm{S},0}:=2\sqrt{2}C_{3}\sqrt{2+L^{-2}_{x}+L^{-2}_{y}}. $$

#### Proof of $C_{\infty}$ .

Define the normalized eigenfunctions of the horizontally periodic Dirichlet Laplacian by

$$ e_{mnk}(x,y,z)=\left(\frac{2}{L_{x}L_{y}}\right)^{1/2}\exp\left[i\left(\frac{2\pi m}{L_{x}}x+\frac{2\pi n}{L_{y}}y\right)\right]\sin(k\pi z). $$

They satisfy

$$ -\Delta e_{mnk}=\lambda_{mnk}e_{mnk}. $$

Set $f=\Delta T$ . Writing

$$ T=\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb{Z}}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\widehat{T}_{mnk}e_{mnk},\qquad f=\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb{Z}}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\widehat{f}_{mnk}e_{mnk}, $$

Green’s identity, horizontal periodicity, and the conditions

$$ T=e_{mnk}=0\qquad\text{on }z=0,1 $$

give

$$ \widehat{f}_{mnk}=-\lambda_{mnk}\widehat{T}_{mnk}. $$

Notice that this identity does not require $f=\Delta T$ to vanish at the boundaries. Consequently,

$$ \nabla T=-\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb{Z}}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{\widehat{f}_{mnk}}{\lambda_{mnk}}\nabla e_{mnk}. $$

Applying the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality with weights $1+\lambda_{mnk}-k^{2}\pi^{2}$ gives

$$ \displaystyle|\nabla T(x,y,z)|^{2}\leq \displaystyle\left[\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb{Z}}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\bigl(1+\lambda_{mnk}-k^{2}\pi^{2}\bigr)|\widehat{f}_{mnk}|^{2}\right] \displaystyle\times\left[\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb{Z}}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{|\nabla e_{mnk}(x,y,z)|^{2}}{\lambda_{mnk}^{\,2}\bigl(1+\lambda_{mnk}-k^{2}\pi^{2}\bigr)}\right]. $$

By Parseval’s identity in the horizontal variables and the completeness of the sine basis in the vertical variable,

$$ \sum_{m,n\in\mathbb{Z}}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\bigl(1+\lambda_{mnk}-k^{2}\pi^{2}\bigr)|\widehat{f}_{mnk}|^{2}=\|f\|_{2}^{2}+\|\nabla_{x,y}f\|_{2}^{2}\leq\|f\|_{H^{1}}^{2}. $$

Furthermore,

$$ |\nabla e_{mnk}(x,y,z)|^{2}=\frac{2}{L_{x}L_{y}}\left[\lambda_{mnk}-k^{2}\pi^{2}\sin^{2}(k\pi z)+k^{2}\pi^{2}\cos^{2}(k\pi z)\right]\leq\frac{2}{L_{x}L_{y}}\lambda_{mnk}. $$

It follows that

$$ |\nabla T(x,y,z)|^{2}\leq\frac{2}{L_{x}L_{y}}\left[\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb{Z}}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\bigl(1+\lambda_{mnk}-k^{2}\pi^{2}\bigr)\lambda_{mnk}}\right]\|\Delta T\|_{H^{1}}^{2}. $$

Taking the supremum over $V$ proves the result. The series converges as the summand behaves as $\lambda_{mnk}^{-2}$ for large wavenumbers. This completes the proof. ∎

#### Proof of $C_{b}$ .

Set

$$ \alpha_{m}=\frac{2\pi m}{L_{x}},\qquad\beta_{n}=\frac{2\pi n}{L_{y}}. $$

The normalized eigenfunctions satisfying homogeneous Dirichlet conditions at $z=0,1$ are

$$ e^{D}_{mnk}(x,y,z)=\sqrt{\frac{2}{L_{x}L_{y}}}\,e^{\mathrm{i}(\alpha_{m}x+\beta_{n}y)}\sin(k\pi z),\qquad k\geq 1. $$

The normalized eigenfunctions satisfying homogeneous Neumann conditions are

$$ e^{N}_{mn0}(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{L_{x}L_{y}}}\,e^{\mathrm{i}(\alpha_{m}x+\beta_{n}y)} $$

for $k=0$ , and

$$ e^{N}_{mnk}(x,y,z)=\sqrt{\frac{2}{L_{x}L_{y}}}\,e^{\mathrm{i}(\alpha_{m}x+\beta_{n}y)}\cos(k\pi z),\qquad k\geq 1. $$

All these functions satisfy

$$ -\nabla^{2}e_{mnk}=\lambda_{mnk}e_{mnk}. $$

The horizontal components have Dirichlet expansions,

$$ B_{i}=\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb{Z}}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\widehat{B}^{i}_{mnk}e^{D}_{mnk},\qquad i\in\{x,y\}, $$

whereas the vertical component has the Neumann expansion

$$ B_{z}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}m,n\in\mathbb{Z},\ k\in\mathbb{N}_{0}\\
(m,n,k)\neq(0,0,0)\end{subarray}}\widehat{B}^{z}_{mnk}e^{N}_{mnk}. $$

The mode $(m,n,k)=(0,0,0)$ is absent because of the zero net-flux condition.

For either horizontal component, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives

$$ \displaystyle|B_{i}(x,y,z)|^{2} \displaystyle\leq\left[\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb{Z}}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\bigl(1+\lambda_{mnk}+\lambda_{mnk}^{2}\bigr)|\widehat{B}^{i}_{mnk}|^{2}\right] \displaystyle\qquad\times\left[\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb{Z}}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{|e^{D}_{mnk}(x,y,z)|^{2}}{1+\lambda_{mnk}+\lambda_{mnk}^{2}}\right]. $$

Since

$$ |e^{D}_{mnk}(x,y,z)|^{2}\leq\frac{2}{L_{x}L_{y}}, $$

the second factor in (A.31) is bounded by $C_{b}^{2}$ .

The same argument for the vertical component gives

$$ \displaystyle|B_{z}(x,y,z)|^{2} \displaystyle\leq\left[\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}m,n\in\mathbb{Z},\ k\in\mathbb{N}_{0}\\
(m,n,k)\neq(0,0,0)\end{subarray}}\bigl(1+\lambda_{mnk}+\lambda_{mnk}^{2}\bigr)|\widehat{B}^{z}_{mnk}|^{2}\right] \displaystyle\qquad\times\left[\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}m,n\in\mathbb{Z},\ k\in\mathbb{N}_{0}\\
(m,n,k)\neq(0,0,0)\end{subarray}}\frac{|e^{N}_{mnk}(x,y,z)|^{2}}{1+\lambda_{mnk}+\lambda_{mnk}^{2}}\right]. $$

The normalized Neumann eigenfunctions satisfy

$$ |e^{N}_{mnk}(x,y,z)|^{2}\leq\frac{2-\delta_{k0}}{L_{x}L_{y}}. $$

Consequently,

$$ |B_{i}(x,y,z)|^{2}\leq C_{b}^{2}\|B_{i}\|_{H^{2}_{\Delta}}^{2}\qquad\text{for }i\in\{x,y,z\}, $$

where

$$ \|\bm{B}\|^{2}_{H^{2}_{\Delta}}:=\|\bm{B}\|^{2}_{2}+\|\nabla\bm{B}\|_{2}^{2}+\|\nabla^{2}\bm{B}\|_{2} $$

Summing over the three components yields

$$ \displaystyle|\bm{B}(x,y,z)|^{2} \displaystyle=|B_{x}|^{2}+|B_{y}|^{2}+|B_{z}|^{2} \displaystyle\leq C_{b}^{2}\left(\|B_{x}\|_{H^{2}_{\Delta}}^{2}+\|B_{y}\|_{H^{2}_{\Delta}}^{2}+\|B_{z}\|_{H^{2}_{\Delta}}^{2}\right) \displaystyle=C_{b}^{2}\|\bm{B}\|_{H^{2}_{\Delta}}^{2}. $$

Taking the essential supremum over $V$ proves the embedding $\|\bm{B}\|_{\infty}\leq C_{b}\|\bm{B}\|_{H^{2}}$ . The series defining $C_{b}$ converges because its summand behaves as $\lambda_{mnk}^{-2}$ for large wavenumbers. ∎

## Appendix B Poloidal-Toroidal Decomposition

If magnetic flux is exact, a magnetic field $\bm{B}$ in the plane layer admits the poloidal-toroidal decomposition

$$ \bm{B}=\nabla\times\nabla\times\Phi\bm{e}_{z}+\nabla\times\Theta\bm{e}_{z}+\bm{B}^{0}=:\bm{B}^{\Phi}+\bm{B}^{\Theta}+\bm{B}^{0}. $$

Respectively, $\Phi$ and $\Theta$ are the scalar potentials for the poloidal and toroidal parts of the magnetic field $\bm{B}^{\Phi}$ and $\bm{B}^{\Theta}$ . In the plane layer, the representation is completed by the (horizontal) base field

$$ \bm{B}^{0}=B^{0}_{x}(z)\,\bm{e}_{x}+B^{0}_{y}(z)\,\bm{e}_{y}. $$

Clearly, for $\alpha\in\{\Phi,\Theta,0\}$ it holds

$$ \nabla\cdot\bm{B}^{\alpha}=0. $$

Here, we establish orthogonality in $L^{2}_{\mathrm{sol}}$ and provide representation formulae.

#### Proposition B.1.

If $\alpha\neq\beta\in\{\Phi,\Theta,0\}$ , then

$$ \langle\bm{B}^{\alpha},\bm{B}^{\beta}\rangle=0. $$

#### Proof.

Writing the volume integral as a vertical integral in $\mathrm{d}z$ of surface integrals in $\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y$ , it follows that

$$ \displaystyle\langle\bm{B}^{\Phi},\bm{B}^{\Theta}\rangle \displaystyle=\int_{0}^{1}\mathrm{d}z\int\bm{B}^{\Phi}\cdot\bm{B}^{\Theta}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y \displaystyle=\int_{0}^{1}\mathrm{d}z\int\nabla_{x,y}\partial_{z}\Phi\cdot\nabla_{x,y}^{\perp}\Theta\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y \displaystyle=-\int_{0}^{1}\mathrm{d}z\int\partial_{z}\Phi\nabla_{x,y}\cdot\nabla_{x,y}^{\perp}\Theta\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y=0. $$

In the last line, we integrated by parts on each surface using that $\nabla_{x,y}$ is tangent to the surface and that $\nabla_{x,y}\cdot\nabla_{x,y}^{\perp}=0$ in general.

For $\alpha\in\{\Phi,\Theta\}$ , it follows that

$$ \displaystyle\langle\bm{B}^{0},\bm{B}^{\alpha}\rangle \displaystyle=\int_{0}^{1}\mathrm{d}z\,\bm{B}^{0}\cdot\int\bm{B}^{\alpha}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y. \displaystyle=\int_{0}^{1}\mathrm{d}z\left(B^{0}_{x}\int B^{\alpha}_{x}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y+B^{0}_{y}\int B^{\alpha}_{y}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y\right)=0. $$

The last equality holds because in either case $\alpha=\Phi$ or $\alpha=\Theta$ , the components $B_{x}^{\alpha}$ and $B_{y}^{\alpha}$ are total derivatives in $\partial_{x}$ or $\partial_{y}$ . ∎

A basic observation is that the toroidal part is $\nabla_{x,y}$ -divergence free

$$ \nabla_{x,y}\cdot\bm{B}^{\Theta}=\partial_{x}B^{\Theta}_{x}+\partial_{y}B^{\Theta}_{y}=0, $$

and the poloidal part is $\nabla_{x,y}$ -curl free

$$ \nabla_{x,y}^{\perp}\cdot\bm{B}^{\Phi}=\partial_{x}B^{\Phi}_{y}-\partial_{y}B^{\Phi}_{x}=0. $$

Clearly, the base part $\bm{B}^{0}$ is annihilated by $\nabla_{x,y}.$

#### Proposition B.2.

The scalar potential for the poloidal part has the representation

$$ \Phi(x,y,z)=\Phi(x,y,0)+\int_{0}^{z}\mathrm{d}z^{\prime}\,(\nabla_{x,y}^{2})^{-1}(\nabla_{x,y}\cdot\bm{B})(x,y,z^{\prime}). $$

#### Proof.

By divergence theorem,

$$ \int\nabla_{x,y}\cdot\bm{B}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y=0. $$

Thus $(-\nabla_{x,y}^{2})^{-1}$ is well defined on every constant $z$ surface. Then

$$ \nabla_{x,y}\cdot\bm{B}=\nabla_{x,y}\cdot\bm{B}^{\Phi}=\nabla_{x,y}^{2}\partial_{z}\Phi. $$

Inverting $\nabla_{x,y}^{2}$ and integrating in $\mathrm{d}z$ yields the claim. ∎

#### Proposition B.3.

The scalar potential for the toroidal part has the representation

$$ \Theta(x,y,z)=(\nabla_{x,y}^{2})^{-1}(\nabla_{x,y}^{\perp}\cdot\bm{B})(x,y,z). $$

#### Proof.

Let us first verify that the $\nabla_{x,y}$ -curl has zero average on each constant $z$ surface. Indeed, after integrating by parts

$$ \int\nabla_{x,y}^{\perp}\cdot\bm{B}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y=\int\mathrm{d}y\int\partial_{x}B_{y}\,\mathrm{d}x-\int\mathrm{d}x\int\partial_{y}B_{x}\,\mathrm{d}y=0 $$

and so $(-\nabla_{x,y}^{2})^{-1}$ in the representation is well defined. Pointwise it holds

$$ \nabla_{x,y}^{\perp}\cdot\bm{B}^{\Phi}=\nabla_{x,y}^{\perp}\cdot\nabla_{x,y}\partial_{z}\Phi=0. $$

Therefore, as claimed

$$ \nabla_{x,y}^{\perp}\cdot\bm{B}=\nabla_{x,y}^{\perp}\cdot\bm{B}^{\Theta}=\nabla_{x,y}^{\perp}\cdot\nabla_{x,y}^{\perp}\Theta=\nabla_{x,y}^{2}\Theta. $$

∎

On the other hand, the poloidal and toroidal part have zero horizontal mean, if $\alpha\in\{\Phi,\Theta\}$ then

$$ \bm{e}_{x}\int B_{x}^{\alpha}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y+\bm{e}_{y}\int B_{y}^{\alpha}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y=0. $$

Almost tautologically,

#### Proposition B.4.

The (horizontal) base part has the representation

$$ \bm{B}^{0}(z)=\bm{e}_{x}\int B_{x}(z)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y+\bm{e}_{y}\int B_{y}(z)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y. $$
